question: For a simple undirected graph with N vertices given by its adjacency matrix A: (1) what does the entry (A^k)_{ij} represent, (2) how can one determine from A whether the graph is connected, and (3) what is the definition of a path between vertices n_i and n_j?

sources.notes: Course textbook. Title page says 214 pages (brief says 216, which is the PDF page count). Printed page = PDF page minus 1; all locators here are printed pages. I viewed page images of printed pp. 11, 21, 22, 23, 48, 49 and read the text layer of pp. 16 and 22 to 23. The text layer drops symbols, so quotes with formulas were copied from the page image and may differ from the text layer in spacing. Book calls a walk 'shrjanc'um', a trail 'chanaparh' (Definition 1.2.12) and a path 'parz chanaparh' (Definition 1.2.13). Per-page text-layer search for the word matrix finds adjacency matrix only on printed pp. 7, 11, 12, 34, 61 (other hits are incidence, total unimodularity and general uses). Not read: the rest of the book. Original textbook, not a review.

sources.notes: Downloaded the full PDF (454 pages) from arxiv.org/pdf/2308.04512 and read Section 2.9 (walks, paths, connectivity for simple graphs), Theorem 4.5.10 with its proof, and the BFS passage. Page numbers are the printed page numbers in the running header of the June 7, 2025 version; they may differ in other versions. Theorem 4.5.10 is stated for multidigraphs, so its use for simple undirected graphs needs the one-step argument that each edge gives two arcs (see claim C5). Lecture-notes text, not peer reviewed; version 3 of a long-lived arXiv text. Original exposition, not a review.

claims.text: Grinberg proves, by induction on k, that for a multidigraph with adjacency matrix C (entry = number of arcs from i to j), the (i,j) entry of C^k equals the number of walks of length k from i to j, including k = 0 (identity matrix).

claims.text: For a simple undirected graph with symmetric 0-1 adjacency matrix A the same count holds: (A^k)_{ij} is the number of walks of length k from n_i to n_j. The paper proves it directly by induction on k (the textbook has no such theorem, see C9); Grinberg's Theorem 4.5.10 is the multidigraph version, and a simple graph is the special case where every edge gives two opposite arcs.

claims.text: Paramadevan and Sotheeswaran, Theorem 2, state the connectivity test: with B = A + A^2 + ... + A^(n-1), the graph is connected if and only if b_ij is nonzero for i different from j.

support.quote: Then, AG is connected if and only if bij 6= 0, when i 6= j.

claims.text: The proof of Theorem 2 in Paramadevan and Sotheeswaran is incomplete: it reads the entry of B as a count of paths (by their Theorem 1, which counts walks) and then passes from a nonzero entry to a path without the walk-to-path lemma. The correct argument needs the lemma (C16, C17) and the length bound (C18).

support.quote: Conversely, if bij 6= 0, then there exist at least one path from vi to vj , thus G is connected.

claims.text: Test: a simple graph on N >= 2 vertices is connected if and only if every off-diagonal entry of A + A^2 + ... + A^(N-1) is positive; equivalently (I + A)^(N-1) has no zero entry. Proof: (A^k)_{ij} counts walks (C5); a walk gives a path of no greater length (C17) and a path has length at most N - 1 (C18); expanding (I + A)^(N-1) by the binomial theorem gives a sum of I and the powers A^k with positive coefficients. Not proved in any source read in the form (I + A)^(N-1).

support.quote: Then, AG is connected if and only if bij 6= 0, when i 6= j.
Then, there is a path from u to v of length ≤ k.

claims.text: Breadth-first search finds shortest paths from a root: the BFS spanning tree has the property that the tree path from the root r to any vertex v is a shortest path from r to v in G. Connectivity by BFS follows by checking whether the tree reaches all vertices; Grinberg states the BFS tree property for multigraphs, not connectivity testing as such.

support.locator: Section on spanning trees, printed p. 176
support.quote: the path from r to v in this spanning tree is a shortest path from r to v in G. For this reason, this spanning tree is called a breadth-first search (“BFS”) tree.

contradictions.summary: Paramadevan and Sotheeswaran Theorem 1 says the entry of A^l counts different paths of length l; Grinberg Theorem 4.5.10 says it counts walks. They differ when a walk repeats a vertex, for example (A^2)_{ii} = d(n_i) > 0 counts walks n_i, n_j, n_i which are not paths.
contradictions.resolution: The paper states walks, proves it, and gives the counterexample; the Paramadevan statement is cited only as a source that confuses the two.

contradictions.summary: The textbook calls a walk with no repeated edge 'path' (1.2.12) and a walk with no repeated vertex 'simple path' (1.2.13); English usage and Grinberg call the second one 'path' and the first one a trail.
contradictions.resolution: Use the course convention (no repeated vertices) for 'path', give a three-column naming table, and cite definition numbers.

contradictions.summary: Textbook Lemma 1.2.1 covers u different from v and gives no length bound; Grinberg Corollary 2.9.7 covers u = v and gives a path of length at most that of the walk.
contradictions.resolution: Complementary, not conflicting. State the lemma with the length bound and the u = v case proved in the paper, citing both.

contradictions.summary: Paramadevan and Sotheeswaran state the connectivity test and prove it by treating walk counts as path counts; the proof is incomplete without the walk-to-path lemma.
contradictions.resolution: State the test, prove it with C5, C17 and C18, and cite Paramadevan for the statement only.
